meta.title: Who really said "Care about what other people think and you will always be their prisoner"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Lao Tzu. It is a paraphrase of Stephen Mitchell's 1988 rendering of Tao Te Ching chapter 9 — a line that is not in the Chinese text at all.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Care about what other people think and you will always be their prisoner'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Lao Tzu, and not in the Tao Te Ching. Stephen Mitchell wrote “Care about people’s approval and you will be their prisoner” in 1988.

answer.label: Not Lao Tzu — a paraphrase of Stephen Mitchell, 1988
answer.authorDates: born 1943 · American poet and translator — his Tao Te Ching appeared in 1988
answer.sourceLine: The sentence people quote is a loosened version of a line by a living American poet. Stephen Mitchell’s 1988 rendering ↗ of Tao Te Ching chapter 9 reads “Care about people’s approval / and you will be their prisoner.” That is Mitchell’s own formulation, not a translation of anything in the Chinese: James Legge’s standard 1891 translation ↗ of the same chapter has no approval and no prisoner in it — and neither word occurs anywhere in Legge’s text. Wikiquote files the line under Laozi/Misattributed ↗ for exactly this reason.

source.excerpt:
Fill your bowl to the brim
and it will spill.
Keep sharpening your knife
and it will blunt.
Chase after money and security
and your heart will never unclench.
Care about people's approval
and you will be their prisoner.

Do your work, then step back.
The only path to serenity.
trail: We read Mitchell’s chapter 9 ↗ directly. It ends: “Chase after money and security / and your heart will never unclench. / Care about people’s approval / and you will be their prisoner. / Do your work, then step back. / The only path to serenity.” The page states its own provenance: “The Tao Te Ching by Lao Tzu, Translated by Stephen Mitchell, 1988.”

Then we checked the Chinese text’s standard English. James Legge’s translation ↗ gives chapter 9 as: “It is better to leave a vessel unfilled, than to attempt to carry it when it is full… When gold and jade fill the hall, their possessor cannot keep them safe. When wealth and honours lead to arrogancy, this brings its evil on itself.” Mitchell’s bowl and knife are recognisable; his prisoner is not there.

The absence is total, not partial: the words “prisoner” and “approval” each occur zero times in the whole of Legge’s text ↗ — all eighty-one chapters. Anyone can repeat that search in a browser’s find box.

Wikiquote’s Laozi page ↗ reaches the same verdict independently, listing this wording among the Misattributed: it “appears in Stephen Mitchell’s rendering into English of Tao Te Ching chapter 9; but this is an interpretation of Mitchell’s which does not appear in the original text or other recognized English translations,” and notes it was “repeated without attribution” in a 2013 self-help book, Hide Your Goat.
source.excerptNote: Chapter 9 in full, from Mitchell’s 1988 version ↗. Note what the popular quotation does to it: “people’s approval” becomes “what other people think,” and an “always” is added that Mitchell did not write. So the line in circulation is a paraphrase of a paraphrase — two removes from any Chinese original.

source.rightsNote: Three layers, and only the top one matters for reuse. The Tao Te Ching itself is ancient and long in the public domain; Legge’s 1891 translation ↗ is public domain too — but neither contains this line. The sentence people quote descends from Stephen Mitchell’s 1988 rendering, which is in copyright. The popular wording itself is an anonymous paraphrase with no identified author. quotle.info makes no public-domain claim for it.

author.name: Stephen Mitchell
author.heading: About Stephen Mitchell
author.bio: Stephen Mitchell is an American poet, translator, scholar and anthologist, born in Brooklyn in 1943, best known for versions of ancient texts that read as English poetry rather than as scholarship — the Tao Te Ching (HarperCollins, 1988), the Bhagavad Gita, Gilgamesh, the Book of Job and Rilke. His Tao Te Ching has reportedly sold over a million copies, which is why its phrasing, rather than any literal translation, is what most English speakers think Lao Tzu sounds like. It is also why lines he composed circulate under Lao Tzu’s name.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most-shared “Lao Tzu” lines on the internet, and it is not in the Tao Te Ching. Two separate things went wrong on the way — the credit, and then the wording.

items.why: The wording is absent from the Chinese text and from recognised English translations — Legge’s 1891 version ↗ contains neither “prisoner” nor “approval” anywhere in its eighty-one chapters. Wikiquote ↗ lists it as misattributed. He may also never have existed: Wikipedia ↗ notes that “some regard the traditional Laozi as largely or wholly legendary.”

Mitchell’s 1988 chapter 9 ↗ reads “Care about people’s approval / and you will be their prisoner.” He is a poet and translator born in 1943 ↗, and his Tao Te Ching is openly a version rather than a literal translation — the interpretation is the point of it.

Even Mitchell did not write the sentence as it is usually quoted. “People’s approval” has become “what other people think,” and an “always” has been added. Wikiquote ↗ records it turning up “repeated without attribution” in a 2013 positive-thinking book, Hide Your Goat.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest credit: Stephen Mitchell, Tao Te Ching chapter 9 (1988) — and if you want his actual sentence, it is “Care about people’s approval and you will be their prisoner” ↗, three words shorter and rather better.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Mitchell’s Tao Te Ching is the reason this happens. It was never presented as a literal translation — it is a poet’s version, and reportedly a million-copy seller ↗, which makes it by far the most-read English “Lao Tzu” there has ever been. When a version that good sells that well, its sentences get quoted as the ancient text rather than as the modern poem they are.

That is the whole mechanism of this misattribution, and it is not unique to this line: a translator’s felicities become the sage’s. The give-away here is the vocabulary. “Approval” as a social currency, and imprisonment by it, is a twentieth-century psychological idea; Legge’s chapter 9 ↗ is talking about overfilled vessels, gold, jade and the danger of arrogance.
detailsBody: Compare the two chapter 9s side by side. Legge (1891) ↗: “It is better to leave a vessel unfilled, than to attempt to carry it when it is full. If you keep feeling a point that has been sharpened, the point cannot long preserve its sharpness… When wealth and honours lead to arrogancy, this brings its evil on itself. When the work is done, and one’s name is becoming distinguished, to withdraw into obscurity is the way of Heaven.” Mitchell (1988) ↗: the bowl, the knife, money and security, approval and prisoners, “Do your work, then step back.” The bones match. The prisoner is Mitchell’s.

None of which makes the sentiment un-Taoist — a reader who likes the line is not being foolish. But “Lao Tzu said it” and “a good modern poet said it about Lao Tzu’s subject” are different claims, and only one of them is true. The historical Laozi ↗ is himself uncertain enough — traditionally 6th century BC, sometimes dated to the 4th, possibly never a single person — that hanging a 1988 sentence on him is doubly a guess.
context.pull: A translator’s felicities become the sage’s. That is how this line was born.

sourcesVerified.claim: Stephen Mitchell's 1988 English version of Tao Te Ching chapter 9 reads in full: "Fill your bowl to the brim / and it will spill. / Keep sharpening your knife / and it will blunt. / Chase after money and security / and your heart will never unclench. / Care about people's approval / and you will be their prisoner. / Do your work, then step back. / The only path to serenity." The page heads itself "The Tao Te Ching by Lao Tzu, Translated by Stephen Mitchell, 1988."

James Legge's translation of chapter 9 reads: "It is better to leave a vessel unfilled, than to attempt to carry it when it is full. If you keep feeling a point that has been sharpened, the point cannot long preserve its sharpness. When gold and jade fill the hall, their possessor cannot keep them safe. When wealth and honours lead to arrogancy, this brings its evil on itself. When the work is done, and one's name is becoming distinguished, to withdraw into obscurity is the way of Heaven." The words "prisoner" and "approval" occur zero times in the entire Gutenberg text (eBook #216, Laozi, trans. James Legge).

Wikiquote's Laozi page lists, under Misattributed, "Care about people's approval and you will be their prisoner" with the variants "Care about what other people think and you will always be their prisoner" and "If you care what people think, you will always be their prisoner", noting it "Appears in Stephen Mitchell's rendering into English of Tao Te Ching chapter 9; but this is an interpretation of Mitchell's which does not appear in the original text or other recognized English translations. Repeated without attribution in Gilliland, Hide Your Goat, a positive thinking book published in 2013."

Wikipedia states "Stephen Mitchell (born 1943) is a poet, translator, scholar, and anthologist", born in Brooklyn, known for translations and adaptations including the Tao Te Ching, published by HarperCollins in 1988, and reports the translation has sold over a million copies.

Wikipedia states that traditional accounts place Laozi in the 6th century BC, sometimes dated 4th century BC, and that "Modern scholars remain divided over his identity, dates, and precise relationship to the received text: some regard the traditional Laozi as largely or wholly legendary, while others consider a historical Lao Dan plausible."
